title: Mobile: Where Mardi Gras Began in America
summary: The Alabama port city founded as the capital of French Louisiana in 1702, where America's first Mardi Gras celebration predates New Orleans by 15 years, and where the Battle of Mobile Bay gave Admiral Farragut his famous battle cry.

content.intro: On March 17, 1699 - the same expedition that named Baton Rouge - French explorers established a settlement at Mobile Bay, making it the capital of French Louisiana. Mobile's Mardi Gras celebration began in 1703, fifteen years before New Orleans even existed. The city changed hands repeatedly: French to British (1763), British to Spanish (1780), Spanish to American (1813). The port grew wealthy shipping cotton; the Civil War made Mobile Bay famous when Admiral David Farragut allegedly shouted 'Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead!' (The torpedoes were actually mines; the quotation may be apocryphal.) The azaleas that bloom in spring earned Mobile its other nickname: Azalea City. But Mardi Gras remains the identity - America's original Fat Tuesday celebration, older than the more famous party 150 miles east.

sections.title: America's Original Mardi Gras
sections.body: New Orleans claims Mardi Gras in the American imagination, but Mobile got there first. French settlers celebrated the pre-Lenten carnival in Mobile beginning in 1703, establishing traditions that would later migrate east when New Orleans was founded in 1718. The Mystic Society of Joe Cain revived Mobile's Mardi Gras after the Civil War; today, more than thirty mystic societies parade through downtown during the two-week carnival season. The throws are different from New Orleans - Moon Pies instead of beads - and the atmosphere is more family-friendly. Mobile's celebration culminates on Fat Tuesday with parades rolling until midnight, when the police sweep the streets clear and Lent begins.

sections.title: The Battle of Mobile Bay
sections.body: By August 1864, Mobile was the last major Gulf Coast port remaining in Confederate hands. Admiral David Farragut led a Union fleet into Mobile Bay to close it. Confederate defenses included Fort Morgan, Fort Gaines, and a field of 'torpedoes' - underwater mines that had already sunk the ironclad USS Tecumseh. According to legend, when warned about the mines, Farragut shouted 'Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead!' and led his fleet through. Whether he actually said those exact words is disputed, but the battle was real: Mobile Bay fell to the Union, and the Confederacy lost its last significant port. Fort Morgan and Fort Gaines remain, open to visitors on the bay's entrance.

sections.title: French Colonial Capital
sections.body: Fort Condé was the center of French Mobile, the administrative capital from which Louisiana was governed before New Orleans took over. The reconstructed fort stands downtown, a reminder of the 60 years when France claimed this coast. The Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, completed in 1850, replaced earlier churches dating to the French colonial era. The Cathedral Square and Bienville Square provide green space in the downtown core. The street layout follows the original French plan, narrow blocks oriented toward the Mobile River. After the Louisiana Purchase, Mobile remained in Spanish territory until Andrew Jackson's forces seized it in 1813 during the War of 1812.

sections.title: Azalea City
sections.body: Mobile's subtropical climate supports spectacular azalea blooms each spring, concentrated in the Azalea Trail Run route and the Bellingrath Gardens 20 miles south of the city. The Azalea Trail Maids - young women in antebellum hoop skirts - serve as official ambassadors for the city, a tradition since 1929 that remains controversial for its romanticized Old South imagery. The live oaks draped in Spanish moss, the wrought-iron balconies, the historic districts - Mobile resembles New Orleans more than it resembles the rest of Alabama. The climate that grows azaleas also brings hurricanes; the city has rebuilt repeatedly after storms, most recently after Hurricane Katrina in 2005.

sections.title: Gateway to the Gulf
sections.body: Mobile Regional Airport (MOB) serves the city with regional connections; Pensacola (PNS) and New Orleans (MSY) offer more options within 60 and 150 miles respectively. I-10 connects Mobile to New Orleans (2.5 hours) and Jacksonville; I-65 runs north to Birmingham and Nashville. The USS Alabama, a World War II battleship, is permanently moored on the causeway across Mobile Bay - a floating museum alongside the submarine USS Drum. From altitude, Mobile appears as a city at the head of Mobile Bay - the port facilities lining the river, the downtown visible as a grid of historic blocks, the causeway stretching east across the bay. What appears from the air as Alabama's only port city is the place where American Mardi Gras began.

content.flightContext: Located at 30.69°N, 88.04°W at the head of Mobile Bay on the Gulf of Mexico coast. From altitude, Mobile appears as a port city at the confluence of the Mobile and Tensaw rivers where they empty into Mobile Bay - the harbor visible with cargo facilities, the downtown grid distinct, the bay stretching south toward the Gulf. What appears from the air as Alabama's only major seaport is the birthplace of American Mardi Gras, the capital of French Louisiana before New Orleans existed.
